concepts.name: Classification of Plastics: Thermoplastics vs. Thermosets and Resin Identification Codes
key_dimensions: Seven resin identification codes (1-PET, 2-HDPE, 3-PVC, 4-LDPE, 5-PP, 6-PS, 7-Others) and their recyclability status
Which plastics are banned vs. permitted under Indian regulations and why
Confusion trap: Not all single-use plastics are thermoplastics; thermosets are non-recyclable by nature
Biodegradable vs. compostable plastics distinction and their regulatory treatment

concepts.name: Single-Use Plastics (SUP): Definition, Banned Items, and Phase-Out Timeline in India
key_dimensions: Exact list of 19 SUP items banned from July 1, 2022 under Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2021
Thickness thresholds: carry bags below 75 microns banned (raised to 120 microns by 2022), non-woven bags below 60 GSM
Trap: PET bottles, multilayer packaging, and plastic milk pouches are NOT in the banned SUP list despite being single-use
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) as the policy tool for non-banned plastic packaging

concepts.name: Plastic Waste Management Rules (PWMR) 2016 and Amendments: Regulatory Architecture
key_dimensions: Shift from Municipal Solid Waste Rules to dedicated PWMR 2016 — key additions like EPR, buy-back mechanisms
2018 amendment: phased elimination of multilayered plastic (MLP) that is non-recyclable/non-energy recoverable
2021 amendment: introduced SUP ban, increased thickness norms, and set up centralized EPR portal
Roles of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) vs. Gram Panchayats vs. producers/importers/brand owners under PWMR

concepts.name: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for Plastic Packaging: Framework and Gaps
key_dimensions: EPR guidelines 2022: four categories of plastic packaging (rigid, flexible, multilayer, compostable) with separate targets
Certificate-based trading system for EPR credits — potential for greenwashing and market manipulation
Trap: EPR is a legal obligation under Environment Protection Act 1986, not just a voluntary scheme
Distinction between EPR for plastic packaging vs. EPR for e-waste, battery waste — different rules apply

concepts.name: Microplastics: Sources, Pathways, and Ecological/Health Impacts
key_dimensions: Primary microplastics (nurdles, microbeads in cosmetics) vs. secondary microplastics (fragmentation of macroplastics)
Pathways: atmospheric deposition, ocean currents, food chain bioaccumulation — detected in human blood, placentas, Arctic ice
Nanoplastics distinction: <1 µm, can cross blood-brain barrier — emerging regulatory concern not yet covered under Indian law
WHO 2022 report: microplastics in drinking water; India's gap in having a permissible limit for microplastics in water standards

concepts.name: Marine Plastic Pollution: Sources, Gyres, and International Governance
key_dimensions: 80% of marine plastic originates from land-based sources; river transport as key pathway (Ganga among top 10 plastic-polluting rivers)
Five major oceanic garbage patches — Great Pacific Garbage Patch is largest but Indian Ocean Gyre is least studied
MARPOL Annex V: prohibits disposal of plastics from ships — India is a signatory but enforcement gaps exist
Trap: UNCLOS does not specifically address plastic pollution; the new BBNJ Agreement (2023) has limited plastic provisions

concepts.name: Global Plastics Treaty (INC Process) under UNEP: Status and India's Position
key_dimensions: UNEA Resolution 5/14 (2022) — mandate for a legally binding global plastics treaty by end of 2024 (INC-5, Busan)
Three negotiating blocs: High Ambition Coalition (full lifecycle approach) vs. Like-Minded Group (India, China, Russia — waste management focus) vs. OPEC nations
India's position: opposes production caps, supports waste management and technology transfer; tension with domestic SUP ban narrative
Comparison trap: This treaty ≠ Basel Convention; Basel already covers plastic waste transboundary movement (2019 amendment)

concepts.name: Basel Convention Amendment 2019 and Plastic Waste Trade
key_dimensions: 2019 Basel Amendment: added plastic waste to Annex II (hazardous and other wastes requiring special consideration) and Annex VIII/IX
Prior Informed Consent (PIC) mechanism now required for export of contaminated/mixed plastic waste to non-OECD countries
Impact on global plastic waste trade: China's 2018 National Sword policy + Basel amendment dramatically reduced plastic waste exports
Trap: Clean, single-type, recyclable plastic waste (e.g., PET) listed in Annex IX — NOT subject to PIC, still tradeable freely

concepts.name: Biodegradable and Compostable Plastics: Standards, Certifications, and Policy Traps
key_dimensions: IS/ISO 17088 standard for compostable plastics in India — must disintegrate in industrial composting conditions (58°C, 90 days)
Trap: 'Biodegradable' is NOT equivalent to 'compostable' — oxo-degradable plastics (with pro-oxidant additives) fragment into microplastics and are banned under PWMR 2021
Compostable plastics permitted but must carry BIS certification and are NOT exempt from EPR obligations
Risk of greenwashing: compostable plastics do not degrade in marine/soil environments without industrial conditions

concepts.name: Plastic Pollution and Human Health: Endocrine Disruptors and Toxic Additives
key_dimensions: Key chemical hazards: BPA (Bisphenol A) in polycarbonate/epoxy resins — endocrine disruptor; phthalates in PVC as plasticizers
PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances) used in food-contact plastics — 'forever chemicals,' not yet regulated in India
Trap: BPA-free plastics often contain BPS or BPF — structurally similar endocrine disruptors; 'BPA-free' label is misleading
Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) regulations on food-grade plastics vs. MoEFCC's PWMR — jurisdictional overlap

concepts.name: Plastic Waste and Climate Change: Carbon Footprint Across the Lifecycle
key_dimensions: Plastics are fossil fuel derivatives — 90% made from virgin petrochemicals; production contributes ~3.4% of global GHG emissions
Waste management emissions: open burning of plastic waste (common in India) releases dioxins, furans, and black carbon — worse than CO2 in short-term warming
Chemical recycling (pyrolysis) presented as climate solution but energy-intensive and produces toxic by-products — greenwashing risk
Trap: Recycling plastics saves energy vs. virgin production, but mechanical recycling downgrades quality — most plastic is only recyclable 1-2 times

concepts.name: Plastic Pollution in Soil (Agroplastics): Mulch Films, Microplastics, and Food Security
key_dimensions: Plastic mulch films widely used in Indian agriculture — accumulate in soil, reduce water infiltration, affect soil microbiome
Microplastics in soil: alter earthworm behavior, reduce crop yield, enter food chain through root uptake
Trap: Biodegradable mulch films are not yet cost-effective or widely available in India; PWMR 2016 does not specifically regulate agroplastics
Emerging concern: nano and microplastics detected in wheat and rice grown in India — food safety regulatory vacuum

concepts.name: Informal Waste Pickers (Kabadiwalas) and the Plastic Recycling Economy in India
key_dimensions: India's informal recycling sector recovers ~60% of plastic waste — largest informal plastic recycling workforce globally
Conflict between EPR formalization and informal sector: EPR credits favor organized recyclers, marginalizing waste pickers
ILO and UNEP recognition of waste pickers as key actors; India's PWMR 2016 acknowledges but does not fully integrate them
Trap: Swachh Bharat Mission focuses on open defecation and cleanliness — it does NOT have a dedicated plastic waste recycling target unlike PWMR

concepts.name: Plastic Roads and Co-Processing: Waste-to-Energy and Material Recovery Options
key_dimensions: MoRTH guidelines mandate use of plastic waste in road construction for roads within 50 km of towns with population >5 lakh
PWMR 2016 Rule 9: waste generators must hand over plastic waste to local body or agencies authorized for co-processing in cement kilns
Trap: Plastic roads use non-recyclable plastic waste (mix of multilayer, non-PET) — not a substitute for recycling hierarchy; incineration in cement kilns releases toxic emissions
Waste-to-energy (WtE) plants: CPCB guidelines permit only MSW-based WtE; dedicated plastic-to-fuel plants face regulatory ambiguity

concepts.name: Constitutional and Legislative Framework Governing Plastic Pollution in India
key_dimensions: Article 48A (DPSP) and Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty) as constitutional basis; Environment Protection Act 1986 as parent legislation for PWMR
Concurrent List Entry 17B (protection of wild animals and birds) and State List Entry 6 (public health, sanitation) — states can legislate on plastic bans independently
Trap: Several states (Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu) had plastic bans before the central PWMR 2021 SUP ban — state bans can be stricter but not weaker than central rules
NGT's role: National Green Tribunal has taken suo motu cognizance of plastic pollution — NGT Act 2010 empowers it to enforce PWMR violations

concepts.name: Plastic Pollution Indices and India's Performance: Metrics and Accountability
key_dimensions: India generates ~3.5 million tonnes of plastic waste annually (CPCB data) — 40% remains uncollected; per capita generation lower than OECD but absolute volume massive
Mismanaged Plastic Waste Index: India ranks high due to open burning and dumping; not the same as 'largest plastic polluter' — trap in interpreting rankings
Plastic Overshoot Day (EA Earth Action report) — India crosses threshold early due to inadequate waste management infrastructure
Trap: India is NOT among top 10 ocean plastic polluters by some recent models (Lebreton 2022) due to inland retention — contrast with older Jambeck 2015 study which ranked India #12

concepts.name: Alternatives to Plastics: Regulatory Promotion, Material Comparison, and LCA Traps
key_dimensions: Government-promoted alternatives: jute bags (Jute Packaging Materials Act 1987 mandates jute for food grains/sugar), cloth bags, areca leaf plates, banana leaf packaging
Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) trap: cotton bags require 7,100 uses to offset carbon footprint of one plastic bag; paper bags have higher water and energy footprint in production
Trap: Replacing plastic with glass/metal increases weight → more transport emissions; plastic's low weight is a genuine environmental advantage in transport sector
Circular economy approach (preferred by UNEP): redesign > reduce > reuse > recycle hierarchy, not simple material substitution

concepts.name: Plastic Pollution and Biodiversity: Impacts on Marine, Terrestrial, and Freshwater Ecosystems
key_dimensions: Ghost fishing gear (derelict nets, traps): responsible for ~46% of Great Pacific Garbage Patch by weight; entanglement of turtles, cetaceans, seabirds
Microplastic ingestion by zooplankton disrupts ocean carbon pump — plastics interfere with biological carbon sequestration (blue carbon connection)

Trap: Plastic pollution is listed as one of three planetary boundaries crises (alongside climate change and biodiversity loss) — but it is NOT yet formally integrated into the CBD Kunming-Montreal Framework targets as a standalone target
Freshwater biodiversity: microplastics detected in Ganga, Yamuna, and Chilika Lake — IUCN Red List species in these habitats face dual threat of habitat loss and plastic ingestion

concepts.name: Plastic Credits and Market-Based Mechanisms: Voluntary vs. Regulatory Instruments
key_dimensions: Plastic credit schemes (voluntary, e.g., Verra's Plastic Program) vs. India's mandatory EPR certificate trading — key distinction in legal enforceability
Risk of double counting: same plastic waste recovery claimed under both voluntary credits and mandatory EPR certificates
Trap: Carbon credits and plastic credits are entirely separate instruments — plastic cleanup does not automatically generate carbon credits unless methane/emissions reduction is quantified
SEBI's ESG disclosure framework now requires large companies to report plastic waste generated and recycled — connects to corporate governance angle
